case_scope.source_excerpt:
A finite statistical microstate model is a pair $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ where $\Omega$ is a finite nonempty set and $\epsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ assigns a finite numerical energy to each microstate. The physical energy of $x\in\Omega$ is $E(x)=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$, with its zero and any retained internal offsets fixed by the declared material model. Energies are evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame specified by [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]], and $U$ is the corresponding macroscopic internal-energy coordinate of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Equal energy values at distinct elements of $\Omega$ count as distinct microstates.

When two such models are declared independent, their joint microstate set is the Cartesian product $\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$, and additivity of the microscopic energy is the explicit condition $\epsilon_{AB}(x,y)=\epsilon_A(x)+\epsilon_B(y)$. Independence and this energy equation are model data; they do not follow merely from the two systems being separated. The definition itself assigns no weights, temperature, probability law, or dynamics.

citations.quote:
A finite statistical microstate model is a pair $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ where $\Omega$ is a finite nonempty set and $\epsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ assigns a finite numerical energy to each microstate. The physical energy of $x\in\Omega$ is $E(x)=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$, with its zero and any retained internal offsets fixed by the declared material model. For a physical internal-energy interpretation, the declared companion mechanical model supplies, for every admitted microstate preparation $x$, a positive total mass and a center-of-mass position map with a defined componentwise velocity at that preparation, obeying the Galilean transformation conditions of [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. That velocity selects the statewise instantaneous rest chart in which $E(x)$ is recorded; a finite set and energy map alone do not construct these mechanical data or a common rest chart for a time interval. Bulk translational kinetic energy and separately tracked external-field energy are excluded from these internal-energy values. The energy zero and any internal offsets are fixed consistently across admitted states. If the statistical model also assigns a single equilibrium macrostate to a preparation, $U$ is its internal-energy coordinate of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]; the pair $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ alone does not assert that macroscopic identification. Equal energy values at distinct elements of $\Omega$ count as distinct microstates.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix an integer $n\ge1$ and an open phase-coordinate domain $O_{\rm phys}\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ with physical canonical coordinates $q_i$ in metres and $p_i$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. The canonical symplectic form on this chart is $\omega_{\rm phys}=\sum_{i=1}^n dq_i\wedge dp_i$. Let $\hat q_i=q_i/(1\,\mathrm m)$ and $\hat p_i=p_i/(1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})$, and let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ be the open image of the chart in these dimensionless coordinates. The corresponding dimensionless canonical form is $\hat\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\hat q_i\wedge d\hat p_i$, so $\omega_{\rm phys}=(1\,\mathrm{J\,s})\hat\omega$.

Let $\hat H:O\to\mathbb R$ be a numerical energy function with continuous partial derivatives through order two, and let $H_{\rm phys}:O_{\rm phys}\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ be $H_{\rm phys}(q,p)=(1\,\mathrm J)\hat H(\hat q,\hat p)$. Where defined, its physical Hamiltonian vector field $X_{H_{\rm phys}}$ is determined by $\iota_{X_{H_{\rm phys}}}\omega_{\rm phys}=dH_{\rm phys}$. For each elapsed time $t$ in its domain, the physical flow map is a function $\phi_t:D_t\to O_{\rm phys}$, where $D_t\subseteq O_{\rm phys}$ is the set of initial data whose trajectories exist through time $t$, and it satisfies $d\phi_t/dt=X_{H_{\rm phys}}\circ\phi_t$. Equivalently, in the dimensionless chart, the flow map $\hat\phi_{\hat t}:\hat D_{\hat t}\to O$ is generated by $X_{\hat H}$ satisfying $\iota_{X_{\hat H}}\hat\omega=d\hat H$, at dimensionless time $\hat t=t/(1\,\mathrm s)$; here $\hat D_{\hat t}$ is the set of initial coordinates whose trajectories exist through $\hat t$. These definitions specify the flow maps when they exist but impose no global-existence or completeness hypothesis on the shell preparation.

A specified open interval $J_E\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a regular compact-shell band when $\hat H^{-1}(K)$ is compact in $O$ for every compact $K\subset J_E$ and $\nabla\hat H$ is nonzero at every point of $\hat H^{-1}(J_E)$.

For $\hat E\in J_E$, the energy shell is $\Sigma_{\hat E}:=\{x\in O:\hat H(x)=\hat E\}$. The graph-chart definition of the weighted shell integral is [[def-tdmath-regular-energy-shell]]: in a local graph chart $x_i=h(z,\hat E)$, its coarea measure is $d\mu_{\hat E}=dA_{\hat E}/|\nabla\hat H|$, with graph-area factor and gradient in the dimensionless Euclidean coordinates. Set $D(\hat E):=\int_{\Sigma_{\hat E}}d\mu_{\hat E}$ and admit the preparation only when $\Sigma_{\hat E}\ne\varnothing$ and $0<D(\hat E)<\infty$. Its normalized shell law is $\nu_{\hat E}(A):=D(\hat E)^{-1}\mu_{\hat E}(A\cap\Sigma_{\hat E})$. The current draft theorem [[thm-tdmath-regular-energy-shell-measure]] proves the coarea identity, chart independence and positive finite shell mass under its stated $C^2$, compact-regular-band hypotheses; its statement and proof are present, while its acceptance remains unresolved. Multiplying the unnormalized shell measure by a fixed positive phase-volume normalization does not change $\nu_{\hat E}$.

For the regular-shell branch below, assume AC as required by
[[def-td-regular-hamiltonian-shell-preparation]] and its coarea-measure
supplier. No choice assumption is needed for the separate finite-window branch.

For a finite microstate model and a declared energy value $E_0$ in joules and resolution $\delta\ge0$ in joules, define the admitted window
$$\Omega_{E_0,\delta}:=\{x\in\Omega:|E(x)-E_0|\le\delta\}.$$
When this set is nonempty, adopt the uniform preparation $P(x)=|\Omega_{E_0,\delta}|^{-1}$ on it and zero outside. Its dimensionless Boltzmann entropy is $\log|\Omega_{E_0,\delta}|$, and its physical entropy convention is $k_{\mathrm B}\log|\Omega_{E_0,\delta}|$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. A zero-width window is allowed only when it contains at least one microstate.

For a continuous classical model, when the regular-band, nonempty-shell, and normalization hypotheses in [[def-td-regular-hamiltonian-shell-preparation]] hold, the microcanonical preparation is the normalized shell measure $\nu_{\hat E}$ defined there. The shell preparation does not require a globally defined flow. These finite-window and regular-shell rules are adopted model preparations. They do not assert Hamiltonian ergodicity, equality with long-time averages, canonical sampling, or equilibration.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(M,\omega)$ be a smooth $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold and $H\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, with Hamiltonian field defined by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$. Wherever its local flow $\phi_t$ is defined, it preserves the symplectic form and the volume measure $m$ determined by $\omega^n/n!$. No completeness is asserted. For a region $R$ on which a nonzero-time map $T=\phi_\tau$ and all its iterates are defined, $T$ is a measure-preserving transformation. If $m(R)<\infty$, then for every measurable $E\subseteq R$, almost every point of $E$ returns to $E$ infinitely often under forward iteration.

If $m(R)=1$ and $T$ is ergodic, then for every $f\in L^1(R,m)$ the averages $N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}f(T^jx)$ converge almost everywhere and in $L^1$ to $\int_Rf\,dm$. Without ergodicity, the limit is the invariant conditional expectation supplied by Birkhoff's theorem, not necessarily the space mean. Finally, if each stated time map $\phi_t$ is a diffeomorphism of a finite invariant region $R$, a density $p_0\ge0$ with $\int_Rp_0\,dm=1$ and $\int_R|p_0\log p_0|\,dm<\infty$ transports by $p_t=p_0\circ\phi_{-t}$ with conserved fine-grained entropy $-k_B\int_Rp_t\log p_t\,dm$, using $0\log0=0$. Volume preservation alone does not imply ergodicity or a time-average/ensemble identity.

Assume AC. Let $O\subset\mathbb R^{2n}$ be open with its canonical symplectic form, let $H\in C^2(O,\mathbb R)$, and let $J\subset\mathbb R$ be open. Suppose $\nabla H\ne0$ on $H^{-1}(J)$ and $H^{-1}(K)$ is compact in $O$ for every compact $K\subset J$. Define $\mu_E$ by [[def-tdmath-regular-energy-shell]]. Then for every nonnegative Borel $f$ compactly supported in $H^{-1}(J)$,
$$\int_Of(x)\,dx=\int_J\mu_E(f)\,dE.$$
For every $E\in J$ with nonempty shell $\Sigma_E=H^{-1}(\{E\})$, $0<\mu_E(1)<\infty$, and $\widehat\mu_E=\mu_E/\mu_E(1)$ is a probability measure. Let $\phi_t$ be a Hamiltonian flow map defined as a diffeomorphism on a full compact energy band containing $\Sigma_E$ and preserving that band. Then $\widehat\mu_E$ is invariant under $\phi_t$ for every such regular $E$. Critical levels and noncompact bands are outside this statement.

The draft suppliers [L1] and [L2] give volume preservation and shell-measure invariance for the matched model in step 1.1. A finite statistical microstate model is a pair $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ where $\Omega$ is a finite nonempty set and $\epsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ assigns a finite numerical energy to each microstate. The physical energy of $x\in\Omega$ is $E(x)=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$, with its zero and any retained internal offsets fixed by the declared material model. For a physical internal-energy interpretation, the declared companion mechanical model supplies, for every admitted microstate preparation $x$, a positive total mass and a center-of-mass position map with a defined componentwise velocity at that preparation, obeying the Galilean transformation conditions of [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. That velocity selects the statewise instantaneous rest chart in which $E(x)$ is recorded; a finite set and energy map alone do not construct these mechanical data or a common rest chart for a time interval. Bulk translational kinetic energy and separately tracked external-field energy are excluded from these internal-energy values. The energy zero and any internal offsets are fixed consistently across admitted states. If the statistical model also assigns a single equilibrium macrostate to a preparation, $U$ is its internal-energy coordinate of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]; the pair $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ alone does not assert that macroscopic identification. Equal energy values at distinct elements of $\Omega$ count as distinct microstates.

When two such models are declared independent, their joint microstate set is the Cartesian product $\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$, and additivity of the microscopic energy is the explicit condition $\epsilon_{AB}(x,y)=\epsilon_A(x)+\epsilon_B(y)$. Independence and this energy equation are model data; they do not follow merely from the two systems being separated. The definition itself assigns no weights, temperature, probability law, or dynamics.

Assign a positive temperature $T$ in kelvins and the exact framework constant $k_{\mathrm B}$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ from [[def-td-si-quantities]], and put $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. For a finite microstate model $(\Omega,\epsilon)$, adopt the canonical preparation
$$P_\beta(x)=\frac{e^{-\beta E(x)}}{Z(\beta)},\qquad Z(\beta)=\sum_{x\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E(x)}.$$
Here $Z$ is dimensionless, positive, and finite because $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty.

The same adopted law may be assigned to a specified countable state model with its stated enumeration and energy list, or to a measurable model $(X,\Sigma,\mu,E)$ with a dimensionless reference measure $\mu$ and measurable energy $E:X\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$, only when $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$ for the declared series or integral. In those cases $P_\beta(i)=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ or the probability density is $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z$ relative to $\mu$. The countable and integral conventions are those of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] at their actual current draft statements.

This is an adopted statistical-mechanical preparation rule. It is not derived from the macroscopic thermodynamic laws, a finite bath, entropy maximization, or a time-evolution equation. It does not assert that a physical sample has this preparation; that identification is an additional model assumption to be tested against a specified preparation and apparatus.

Take $\Omega$ to be a finite nonempty microstate set as in [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: distinct elements count as distinct microstates, and the physical energy values are finite and measured in joules in the declared rest frame. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and stage energy functions $E_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ for $k=0,\ldots,m$, with the energy offsets fixed by the declared protocol model. Fix inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$. The finite partition sum and canonical probability vector at stage $k$ are $Z_k=\sum_{i\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E_k(i)}$ and $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$. Since $\Omega$ is nonempty and finite and each energy is finite, $0<Z_k<\infty$ and $\pi_k$ is a strictly positive probability vector.

A transition kernel at stage $k$ is a matrix $K_k(i,j)\ge0$ with $\sum_{j\in\Omega}K_k(i,j)=1$. In the forward stage order, the energy changes instantaneously from $E_{k-1}$ to $E_k$ while the state is still $i_{k-1}$; the subsequent bath transition samples $i_k$ using $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$ at fixed energy $E_k$. A path is $\omega=(i_0,\ldots,i_m)\in\Omega^{m+1}$. For an initial law $\mu_0$, its path probability is $P_F(\omega)=\mu_0(i_0)\prod_{k=1}^mK_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$.

Work on the system is positive when energy is supplied to it, and heat into the system is positive when a bath transition raises its energy. Define $W(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$ and $Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_k)-E_k(i_{k-1})]$, both in joules. Define $F_k=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_k$ and $\Delta F=F_m-F_0=-\beta^{-1}\log(Z_m/Z_0)$. These are finite-model quantities; their physical interpretation is conditional on the adopted preparation and transition assumptions.

citations.quote: Choose a Galilean inertial chart $\mathcal F$ as defined in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]] for the specified fixed closed trap-and-bath body, assumed to have positive total mass and the center-of-mass map required there, and supply its componentwise differentiable center-of-mass trajectory on the whole modeled time interval. Assume that its center-of-mass velocity is one constant vector on that interval, so the single constant boost of that supplier selects $\mathcal F$ with zero center-of-mass velocity throughout. Take $\mathcal F$ to be this common rest chart. The trap-and-bath background is held fixed in this idealization; center-of-mass recoil or accelerating-frame dynamics are not part of the scalar process. In this chart let $\mathbf r_c\in\mathbb R^3$ be the fixed trap-center position and let $\mathbf e\in\mathbb R^3$ be a fixed unit vector along the modeled trap axis. For a particle position $\mathbf r\in\mathbb R^3$, define the signed displacement $x=\langle\mathbf r-\mathbf r_c,\mathbf e\rangle$ in metres; the process $X_t$ in [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]] is this coordinate of the particle position at time $t$. Thus $U(x)=kx^2/2$ is the harmonic potential relative to the trap center, not an absolute spatial coordinate. Using the SI conventions and exact $k_{\mathrm B}$ of [[def-td-si-quantities]], take stiffness $k>0$ in joules per square metre, constant mobility $\mu>0$ in square metres per joule-second, and bath temperature $T_b>0$ kelvin. Adopt the one-dimensional overdamped model $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, interpreted through the integral equation of [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]], with $\gamma=\mu k$ in seconds$^{-1}$ and $\sigma^2=2\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b$ in square metres per second. Here $B$ is standard Brownian motion with its stated filtration and increment hypotheses, and the bath noise is independent of the initial preparation. This Einstein noise relation and the linear Markov model are physical assumptions. They do not follow from equilibrium thermodynamics alone and do not report a measured spectrum or calibration.

Assume the filtered probability space, Brownian increment hypothesis, and initial data of [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]], including $\mathbb E X_0^2<\infty$ and future increments independent of $\mathcal F_0$. For $\gamma,\sigma>0$, on every finite time interval the process
$$X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sigma e^{-\gamma t}\int_0^t e^{\gamma s}\,dB_s$$
has a continuous adapted version, solves the stated Ornstein–Uhlenbeck integral equation, and is the unique continuous solution driven by the same $(X_0,B)$. Put $V=\sigma^2/(2\gamma)$. For $0\le s<t$, its transition law conditional on $\mathcal F_s$ is normal with mean $e^{-\gamma(t-s)}X_s$ and variance $V(1-e^{-2\gamma(t-s)})$. Consequently
$$\mathbb E X_t=e^{-\gamma t}\mathbb E X_0,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=e^{-2\gamma t}\operatorname{Var}(X_0)+V(1-e^{-2\gamma t}).$$
From any such initial law, $X_t$ converges in distribution to $N(0,V)$. If $X_0\sim N(0,V)$ and is independent of future Brownian increments, the process is stationary Gaussian with covariance $C(\tau)=Ve^{-\gamma|\tau|}$, and its transition kernel satisfies detailed balance with the $N(0,V)$ density. Its transition density solves the Fokker–Planck equation for positive time. Under the convention $S(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}C(\tau)e^{i\omega\tau}\,d\tau$, the stationary spectrum and time-average bound are
$$S(\omega)=\frac{V\gamma}{\pi(\gamma^2+\omega^2)},\qquad\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac1T\int_0^T X_t\,dt\right)\le\frac{2V}{\gamma T}.$$
All these statements concern the specified linear stochastic model. An Einstein relation between $\sigma$ and a physical bath temperature would be an additional physical postulate.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$ carry a standard Brownian motion $B$ adapted to the filtration, with future increments independent of the present sigma-algebra. $$X_t=X_0-\gamma\int_0^tX_s\,ds+\sigma B_t,$$
where the time integral is the ordinary Lebesgue integral along the continuous path. In differential notation this is $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, with the stochastic differential interpreted through the displayed integral equation.

The definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. The Itô integral in the explicit representation is the square-integrable predictable-process integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]].
